To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the A-I concentration difference for glucose and lactate is reduced during insulin infusion, but that the effect is diminished when the muscle is shortened.

passive muscle shortening in the hyperinsulinemic state diminishes the interstitial glucose concentration gradient, increases the interstitial lactate gradient, and has no effect on the interstitial insulin gradient.
the muscle arterial-interstitium concentration differences of glucose and lactate, but not of insulin, are diminished during PSL in hyperinsulinemic rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of muscle movement on the microcirculation in rat muscle.
the transcapillary transport of insulin, glucose, and lactate and how this is influenced by passive muscle shortening.
the transcapillary transport of insulin and glucose in skeletal muscle in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PSL increases the transcapillary glucose flux and the muscle uptake of glucose, but not the insulin-mediated uptake of glucose.
PSL increases blood flow and the transcapillary flux of lactate and glucose but not that for insulin.
PSL in the insulin-stimulation state increases capillary permeability, blood flow, and glucose uptake but does not affect the insulin uptake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transcapillary transport of insulin and glucose, but not of lactate, is rate limiting for glucose uptake and that PSL increases the rate of transport.

the A-I concentration differences of glucose and insulin are not affected by PSL in the basal state, whereas in the hyperinsulinemic state they are affected by PSL, and that the A-I lactate concentration difference is affected by PSL both in the basal state and in the hyperinsulinaemic state.
passive muscle shortening increases blood flow and the capillary permeability for insulin and glucose, but not for lactate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
passive muscle shortening increases blood flow and glucose transport in muscle.
PSL, in combination with insulin stimulation, increases the transcapillary transport of glucose and lactate, whereas that of insulin is unaffected.
the muscle capillaries are not a barrier for the transcapillary transport of insulin.
